source.title: Neural Scaling Laws for Learning-Based Identification of Nonlinear Systems
source.authors: M. Roschkowski; K. Cherifi; Hannes Gernandt

record.file_problem: None. The text is complete and readable; it contains minor typographical and formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in a different learning task and refines the simple-law picture with results on broken curves, saturation, and sensitivity to the number of fitted breaks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling sweeps and fitted error curves for system-identification models. It cites language-model scaling results only as background; those cited results are not recorded here. Many additional outcomes appear only in overview plots and are not separately quantified in the text.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own resource sweeps (about 63k input-state-output jobs plus input-output jobs) for neural system-identification models. It fits broken saturated power laws of error against compute, data and parameter count. This is a new, non-language setting with direct results on whether the power-law form holds there (V5). The break-count and saturation results bear on curves bending away from a single power law (V7). It is not mainly a refutation, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim the NSLs are largely independent of architecture and physical priors. They claim very long training (up to 2^14 epochs) still improves error. The anticipation of resource needs from early trends is asserted, not validated on held-out larger runs.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains neural models for nonlinear system identification and fits broken laws to normalized MAE/MSE over compute, data, or parameter sweeps. It uses lower-envelope fitting and does not use language-model held-out cross-entropy or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted curve and its apparent scaling depend on resource (compute, data, or parameters), error metric (nMAE versus nMSE), system and architecture, and the chosen number of breaks. The authors also specify a lower-envelope construction and manual initialization for a non-convex fit.

fits_no_version.finding: Model-size NSLs saturate at small parameter counts (~10^3) across all systems. The authors conclude data matters more than model size, contrasting this with NLP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small-data scientific regression tasks, parameter scaling saturates early and data is the binding resource.

fits_no_version.finding: Training for up to 2^14 epochs on the same data still reduces error (multi-epoch regime).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Error keeps falling with heavily repeated epochs in system identification.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Open Journal of Control Systems (venue stated; review status not stated)
record.problems: The experiments assume noise-free, exactly known state-space equations for simulated data. For input-output cases, test error is measured at the last training iteration rather than selected using validation scores. The fitted laws use a lower envelope of observed outcomes, fitting is non-convex and manually initialized, and the authors note that choosing the number of breaks can be ambiguous. No statistical uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: The overview plots in Appendix C (Figures 12–17) and Appendix D (Figures 18–23) contain many additional architecture/system/metric curves. Their individual numeric values are not stated in the text, so those plot-only series are not separately cataloged; the text's aggregate observations are noted in gate_note and the authors' conclusion.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss is not studied.

No forecast from small runs is checked against held-out larger runs. The authors claim early trends allow anticipation but only fit observed envelopes. r4 notes a late break would defeat extrapolation.
No fixed-compute optimal allocation of parameters versus data is computed.
Depth and width at fixed parameter count are not isolated. Architecture-family comparisons (unstructured, input-affine, port-Hamiltonian) are not shape comparisons.
Image and video models, fine-tuning and transfer are untested. Repeated data (many epochs) is only touched qualitatively.
Published language-model exponent disagreements, parameter-counting conventions and compute-optimal splits are untested.

missing.what: Aggregate text statements: all model NSLs (nMAE and nMSE, both data types) saturate at low parameter counts, and all input-output compute NSLs saturate above 10^12 flops. These are stated in words, not just plotted.
Metric dependence: nMSE NSLs show more outliers and more variation than nMAE, and the authors say nMAE seems the more natural metric.
Claim that NSLs are largely independent of architecture: compute-nMAE curves look very similar across architectures and datasets.

record.verdict_notes: Laws are fitted to a lower envelope of many runs that co-vary the other resources, with test error taken at the last iteration. Fits are non-convex and manually initialized, and no uncertainty is reported. Scales are tiny (≤~10^4 parameters, ≤~10^5 data points). Saturation in r6, r7 and r10 is attributed by the authors to data limits, so it does not contradict a power law under non-bottlenecked conditions. V7 links rest on bending and fitting-choice evidence in a non-language setting.

versions.untested_parts: It does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy in language models.

It does not evaluate forecasts from fits on small runs against separately held-out, orders-of-magnitude-larger runs. It fits curves to the observed outcome envelopes and discusses possible anticipation.
It does not find or compare loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute.
It compares scaling behaviour across architectures, but does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
It tests system-identification tasks, not image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
It measures system-identification evaluation errors, not downstream task performance or its predictability from pretraining loss.

It does not compare published language-model exponents or test how parameter-count conventions affect compute-optimal allocations. Its fitting-sensitivity results concern the choice of number of breaks and the study's system-identification setups.

rows.subject: input-affine architecture on the ball system
rows.size_stated: Model parameters varied; exact range not stated for this fit.
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute–nMAE scaling curve across training runs.
rows.measure: nMAE as a function of compute
rows.value: Fitted broken law has b = 2 and margin M = 0.04; the text describes a plateau until roughly 10^6 flops, then a short steep segment and a long approximately power-law segment through roughly 10^12 flops.
rows.note: The reported curve is broken rather than one power law across the full range. The paper says scaling is highly predictable over roughly 10^7 to 10^12 flops for the configurations considered.
rows.check: For V5, the authors report an approximately linear log-log segment over ~10^7–10^12 flops after an initial plateau, which is the saturated power-law form, so 'observed' rather than 'partial'. For V7 the two breaks show bending away from one power law. The text says 'using one break' but reports b = 2; the record correctly uses b = 2.

rows.subject: input-affine architecture on the ball system
rows.size_stated: Model parameters varied; exact range not stated for this fit.
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute–nMSE scaling curve across training runs.
rows.measure: nMSE as a function of compute
rows.value: Fitted broken law has b = 2 and margin M = 0.09; breaks are at similar compute budgets to the nMAE fit.
rows.note: The authors report fewer points close to the envelope above 10^10 flops for nMSE than for nMAE.
rows.check: Same shape as r1, but fewer runs sit near the envelope above 10^10 flops for nMSE, so the fit is weaker. This is more about metric choice than about bending; V7 removed.

rows.subject: unstructured architecture on the motor system
rows.size_stated: Model parameters varied; exact range not stated for this fit.
rows.operation_detail: Fit a data–nMAE scaling curve across training runs.
rows.measure: nMAE as a function of data size
rows.value: Fitted broken law has b = 2 and margin M = 0.07; the text describes a smooth-scaling range from about 8,000 to 64,000 data points.
rows.note: The paper says compute and model size also affect whether runs lie near the fitted envelope.
rows.check: Smooth scaling from 8,000 to 64,000 points, which the authors call high-confidence. This is under one order of magnitude of clean range. The formula prints 'C' for the data variable.

rows.subject: input-affine architecture on the spring system
rows.size_stated: Model parameters varied; exact range not stated for this fit.
rows.operation_detail: Fit a data–nMAE scaling curve across training runs.
rows.measure: nMAE as a function of data size
rows.value: Fitted broken law has b = 2 and margin M = 0.07; the text identifies a break at about 10^4 data points.
rows.note: The authors say performance beyond this break cannot be predicted solely from experiments below about 10^4 data points.
rows.check: A break at ~10^4 data points means performance beyond it is not predictable from smaller runs. This is a bend at large scale (V7 observed).

rows.subject: port-Hamiltonian architecture on the ball system
rows.size_stated: Model parameters varied; exact range not stated for this fit.
rows.operation_detail: Fit a model-size–nMAE scaling curve across training runs.
rows.measure: nMAE as a function of parameter count
rows.value: Fitted broken law has b = 1 and margin M = 0.11; the text says scaling beyond about 10^3 parameters does not improve results.
rows.note: The paper also says models that are too small, or runs with insufficient data or compute, do not achieve good performance.
rows.check: The model-size curve saturates at ~10^3 parameters. Data and compute were also co-varied, so saturation may reflect a data bottleneck that V5 (via V1) excludes.

rows.subject: SUBNET on the Silverbox system
rows.size_stated: Model parameters varied; exact range not stated for this fit.
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute–nMAE scaling curve across training runs.
rows.measure: nMAE as a function of compute
rows.value: Fitted broken law has b = 1 and margin M = 0.02; the curve strongly saturates above 10^12 flops.
rows.note: The authors infer that additional compute on this dataset is unlikely to improve results substantially.
rows.check: Strong saturation above 10^12 flops, which the authors attribute to the bounded real dataset (a data bottleneck).

rows.subject: NARX on the Wiener-Hammerstein system
rows.size_stated: Model parameters varied; exact range not stated for this fit.
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute–nMAE scaling curve across training runs.
rows.measure: nMAE as a function of compute
rows.value: Fitted broken law has b = 3 and margin M = 0.05; all three breaks occur between 10^7 and 10^9 flops, and the curve strongly saturates above 10^12 flops.
rows.note: The text describes strong saturation at high compute rather than one power law over the whole range.
rows.check: Three breaks between 10^7 and 10^9 flops, then saturation above 10^12 flops. For V7 this is clear bending (observed).

relationships.condition: Neural system identification: compute sweeps on simulated systems (input-state-output) and data sweeps on benchmark systems (input-output), nMAE
relationships.reason: Saturated or broken power laws with long smooth log-linear segments: r1 (~10^7–10^12 flops), r3, r8, r9.
relationships.display_finding: Normalized MAE followed saturated or broken power laws with long smooth log-linear segments, including a compute sweep spanning approximately 10^7–10^12 FLOPs.

relationships.condition: Model-size sweeps, high-compute input-output runs, late data breaks, and the nMSE metric
relationships.reason: Model-size curves saturate near 10^3 parameters (r5, r10). Compute saturates above 10^12 flops on real benchmarks (r6, r7). A break at 10^4 data points (r4) and a weaker nMSE fit (r2) also qualify the form.
relationships.display_finding: Model-size curves saturated near 10³ parameters and compute gains above 10¹² FLOPs, alongside a break near 10⁴ data points and a weaker nMSE fit.

relationships.condition: Broken-law fits in system identification, including the spring-system compute fit at 1–4 breaks
relationships.reason: Curves need 2–4 breaks (r1, r4, r7), and fit quality depends on the chosen break count, with M ranging 0.68 to 0.03 and the authors calling the choice ambiguous (r11–r14).
relationships.display_finding: Curves required 2–4 breaks, and M ranged from 0.68 to 0.03 as the chosen break count changed.
